fields.meta_title: Map Quiz Maker: Build a Quiz Played on Your Map | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Use a map quiz maker that builds click-the-map quizzes on your own map, scores every answer, and saves each click to a database you own.
fields.h1: Build a Map Quiz Maker That Scores Every Click
fields.hero_description: Build quizzes with a map quiz maker that scores each click on your map and saves every answer to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Map Quiz
fields.features_subheading: A map quiz asks players to find a place, not name it. Emergent builds the map, the scoring, and the table behind them from a prompt.
fields.feature_1:
Answers given with a click on the map

Upload your own map or describe the one you need, and Emergent builds a quiz where each answer is a click on a region. The app scores that click against the region you marked right.
fields.feature_2:
A row for every click

Every answer lands as a row in a database you own, with the player, the question, the region clicked, and the time. Sort by question to see where the wrong clicks pile up.
fields.feature_3:
Pass marks that send an email

Set a pass mark, such as 11 of 12, and the app emails you the name of each player who falls short, or posts the list to Slack. Players who pass go straight to their score screen.
fields.feature_4:
One question per screen on a phone

Players answer one question per screen, so the map fills a phone and a tap counts as the click. Emergent puts no cap on how many people play it, in one class or across fifty.
fields.feature_5:
Leaderboards ranked by score, then time

Ask for a leaderboard, and Emergent builds one that ranks teams by score and breaks ties on time. A follow-up prompt changes the round length or the points for a hard region.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and the full code

Run the quiz on your own domain; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep building on it.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Map Quizzes and What Each Caught
fields.tab_content_1:
Delaware stumped 39 students, more than any state

Every student in Greta Osterhout's 3 social studies sections at Tamarack Middle School clicks all 50 states on a blank US map. Of her 84 students, 39 placed Delaware wrong, more than any other state. Rhode Island came next at 31. She gave Monday's class to the Mid-Atlantic before the unit test.
fields.tab_content_2:
Below 11 correct zones, no solo route yet

New drivers at Ruskmoor Couriers click each of the company's 12 delivery zones on a city map before their first solo route. The pass mark is 11 of 12. Last week 3 of 9 new hires fell short, and dispatcher Owen Takahara got an email naming them. Each rode along with a senior driver for one more day, then retook the quiz.
fields.tab_content_3:
Creek or ridge: 460 hikers took the wrong loop

Hikers who reach the trailhead at Kestrel Bend Preserve take an 8-question trail map quiz on a phone, using the code on the sign. This fall brought 1,120 tries. Asked where the waterfall sits, 460 hikers picked the Ridge Loop, though the falls are on the Creek Loop. Rangers redrew the trailhead map with the falls marked.
fields.tab_content_4:
16 teams ranked by score, then by time

Trivia night at Brass Kettle Taproom ends with a map round. Each of the 16 teams drops 10 pins on a world map from one phone. The leaderboard ranks teams by correct pins and breaks ties on time. Lost Latitudes and Pint Meridian both scored 9 of 10, and Lost Latitudes took the round at 3:12 to Pint Meridian's 3:47.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Map Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan a map quiz, set how it scores, and build it with Emergent's map quiz maker.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the map before the questions
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Mark one right region per question
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Choose a pass mark or a ranking
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose the map players will click, such as a blank US outline, your city's delivery zones, or a trail map. Upload it or describe it in your prompt. The map decides how many regions a player can click and how small the smallest one gets.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write each question as a place to find, such as a state or a trail junction, and mark the one region that counts as correct. Enlarge tiny regions, like Rhode Island on a US map, so a player on a phone can tap them without zooming.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Settle whether a click must land inside the region or only near it, and whether a player gets a second try. One try per question keeps scores comparable between groups. Put the rule in your prompt so the scoring matches it.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Training quizzes need a pass mark and a person who hears about anyone below it. Games need a ranking instead: correct answers first, then time to break ties. Decide which kind your quiz is before you build it, since the results view differs.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the quiz in one prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the map, the questions, the scoring rule, and the pass mark or leaderboard in a single prompt. Emergent builds the quiz and the database behind it, and a follow-up prompt changes either one when a question needs work.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Before launch, have five people take the quiz on their own phones. Watch for a region that is hard to tap or a question two people read two different ways. Fix each one by prompt, then clear their test answers from the table.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Read the misses and act on them
fields.howto_step_7_des: After the first round, sort the answers by question. A region missed far more than the rest points to a lesson to reteach or a sign to redraw. Run the same quiz again later to see whether the change moved the score.
